content: This experiment compares five configurations of a 512-expert MoE model (Qwen3.8-27B) on knowledge retention and code generation after aggressive compression. The arms range from a full 512-expert Q2_K_XL checkpoint (73.5 GiB) down to a dense 27B Q6_K (21.3 GiB), with two pruned 320-expert variants at Q2 and Q3 in between, plus a 512-expert IQ1_S quantization. Pruning 192 experts at Q2 drops raw knowledge accuracy by roughly 20 percentage points (55.0% to 35.2%, p = 5e-21) and pushes fabrication to nearly half of all committed answers, while refusal stays near zero. At matched model size, quantizing all 512 experts to IQ1_S beats the pruned Q3 variant by 22.8 points on knowledge (p = 1e-30). The anticipated domain split—pruning hurting knowledge but sparing code—did not materialize: the 1-bit unpruned model ties the pruned model on HumanEval+ (93.9% vs 92.7%) while dominating on knowledge. The dense 27B Q6_K, at 21.3 GiB, lands at 77.6% committed accuracy and 92.1% HumanEval+. All experimental gates passed with no VBR degradation on any arm.

content: An experiment on an RX 9070 XT (ROCm) compared variable-bit-rate (VBR) KV-cache quantization against static q8_0 and q4_0 using Qwen3.5-9B-Q8_0 (a hybrid model where only 8 of 32 layers store KV, D=256) on wikitext-2 at 32k context, teacher-forced KLD against an f16 reference. At matched VRAM (~544 MiB), frozen VBR achieved 71% lower mean KLD than static q8_0 (0.000644 vs 0.002237), winning all 9 chunks (p = 0.0039). Before memory pressure, frozen VBR was bit-identical to f16 across all 69,120 pre-knee positions. Two negative results stood out: allocating extra bits to V rather than K made things 48% worse at equal bytes, and q4_0's excess error over q8_0 did not grow with sequence depth. The critical caveat: unfrozen VBR handled the first 32k chunk well (KLD 0.0001) but then degraded every subsequent chunk to the 1.25-bpv floor (KLD 0.13, 60× worse than q8_0). At 288 MiB, however, unfrozen V4 never hit the problem and was bit-identical to its frozen counterpart. The author discloses a collaboration with VBR's developer.

This preregistered experiment tested whether Multi-Token Prediction (MTP), a decode-time acceleration technique, changes outcomes for LLM agents. Each arm ran 120 item-seeds. MTP-off scored a 75.0% pooled pass rate; MTP-on scored 69.2%, a mean difference of −5.8 pp (95% CI [−12.2, +0.5], sign-flip p = 0.12). The preregistered equivalence test at ±10 pp was not met and harm was not detected at α = .05, so the verdict is inconclusive. No timeouts occurred in either arm.

Descriptively, outcome flips lean against MTP: 9 of 13 flips into or out of a wrong-action label go into it under MTP, typically where MTP-off would have asked for clarification. MTP also showed lower cross-seed consistency (23.7% vs. 17.2% within-arm disagreement).

Of 120 paired runs, 85% had a different trajectory but the same outcome, with +0.14 tool calls on average. The 12.5% of runs where the outcome actually flipped ran 11:4 against MTP, and 9 of those 11 were irreversible wrong actions. The authors note that for retryable, verifiable work the relevant metric is expected time to success, which would require a separate caching-on time-to-completion run.

The only variable between arms was the sampling draw. Out of 29 scorable items the two arms disagreed on 3, yielding a noise floor of 10.3%. That is exactly the discordance rate measured in a separate run comparing Q6_K against a 3.5 bpw quant (AD-IQ3_S), which also produced 3 out of 29 disagreements. Two runs of the same model therefore disagree just as often as a Q6_K disagrees with a 3.5 bpw quant, and both splits are near-symmetric, the signature of pure sampling rather than a real effect. Aggregate pass rates across three arms of the same file spanned 10.4 points. The author concludes that every quant comparison the campaign produced—measured deltas of 13.9%, 12.1%, 22.2%, 27.6%, and 10.3%—sits at or below the 10.3% noise floor and is void, not merely underpowered. The instrument, as configured (one rep, temp 1.0), has no demonstrated discriminating power. The corpus construction was validated independently and is not implicated.

# VBR full-reset at chunk boundary cascades into immediate turbo1_tcq degrade of all KV tensors (quality collapse from chunk 2 onward)

## Summary

On a ROCm build (commit `38ada0e1b`), running `llama-perplexity` with `-ctk vbr -ctv vbr --vbr-vram 2048M` and `--chunks 2`, the VBR subsystem performs a **full reset** at the chunk-1 → chunk-2 boundary even though projected KV usage (552 MiB) is well under the 2048 MiB budget. In the same millisecond the reset lands, a cascade of degrades fires at **0 cells**, walking every KV tensor down to `turbo1_tcq` before chunk 2 has processed a single token. From chunk 2 onward the mean KLD vs. f16 is ≈ 0.13, compared to 0.0022 for a static `q8_0` KV cache at the same context length.

## Reproduction

**Hardware / build:** ROCm build, commit `38ada0e1b`, AMD RX 9070 XT (also the desktop display GPU).

**Command:**

```bash
HIP_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 llama-perplexity \
  -m Qwen_Qwen3.5-9B-Q8_0.gguf \
  -f wiki.test.raw \
  -ngl 99 -fa on \
  -c 32768 -b 512 -ub 512 \
  -v --chunks 2 \
  -ctk vbr -ctv vbr \
  --vbr-vram 2048M
```

**What to look for in the log:**

1. Chunk 1 – first VBR degrade fires at **25 088 cells**.
2. End-of-chunk-1 line: `projected 552.00 / budget 2048.00 MiB (mapped 574.50) at 32768 cells`
3. Immediately after: `VBR full reset: cache empty -- 15 tensors back at their entry tier`
   (the model has 16 KV tensors: 8 layers × K/V)
4. In the **same millisecond**, degrades #1 … #N fire at **0 cells**, walking every tensor to `turbo1_tcq` before chunk 2 has any tokens.
5. From chunk 2 onward, mean KLD vs. f16 ≈ **0.13**.

## Observed vs. Expected

| | Observed | Expected |
|---|---|---|
| VBR full reset at chunk boundary | Fires even though projected usage (552 MiB) ≪ budget (2048 MiB) | No reset; the cache should still be well within budget |
| Post-reset degrade cascade | All tensors degrade to `turbo1_tcq` at 0 cells, before chunk 2 processes a token | No degrade (or at most a mild one) given the large headroom |
| Quality from chunk 2 | Mean KLD ≈ 0.13 vs. f16 | Comparable to static `q8_0` (KLD ≈ 0.0022) |

- **Not a VRAM-pressure issue.** Free VRAM sampled every 0.5 s never dropped below **3 903 MiB** during the run.

- `llama-server` (the above was reproduced only via `llama-perplexity`).

Why does the VBR subsystem issue a "full reset: cache empty" and immediately re-degrade every tensor to `turbo1_tcq` at 0 cells when the projected KV footprint is only ~27 % of the configured budget? The 15-tensor reset (out of 16) and the 0-cell degrade cascade suggest the chunk-boundary cache-clear path is interacting incorrectly with the VBR tier ladder.

# Tool-call arguments corrupted: qwen3-coder parser mis-routed for MiMo-V2.6-Distill-Qwen-9B (compact `</parameter>` rendering)

## Summary

`chat.cpp` (line 1213) selects the tool-call parser by substring-matching the **template source** for `"<tool_call>"`, `"<function="`, and `"<parameter="`. The MiMo-V2.6-Distill-Qwen-9B (Q8_0) chat template contains all three substrings, so requests are routed to the **qwen3-coder** parser. That parser hardcodes the literal `"\n</parameter>\n"` as the parameter-closing delimiter, but MiMo's template renders parameters **compactly** (no surrounding newlines). The mismatch corrupts parsed arguments on multi-call turns.

## Reproduction steps

1. Serve `MiMo-V2.6-Distill-Qwen-9B` (Q8_0) via the `llama.cpp` server.
2. Use the model's shipped chat template, which emits tool calls as:
   ```
   <tool_call><function=NAME><parameter=KEY>value</parameter>...
   ```
   (note: no `\n` before or after `</parameter>`).
3. Issue a prompt that elicits **multiple** tool calls in a single turn.
4. Inspect the parsed arguments returned by the server.

## Observed behaviour

- 6 of 10 multi-call turns returned corrupted arguments.
- In a larger run: **17 of 30** multi-call turns were corrupted.

## Expected behaviour

All tool-call arguments are parsed correctly regardless of whether the template renders `</parameter>` with or without surrounding newlines.

## Workaround (validated)

Replacing the literal `"<parameter="` in the template source with the split form `'<param' ~ 'eter='` causes the substring check at `chat.cpp:1213` to **fail**, so the generic auto-parser is used instead of the qwen3-coder parser. The rendered template output is **byte-identical** to the original.

With this workaround in place, corruption dropped from **17/30 → 0/30** (p = 6.2 × 10⁻⁷).

## Ruled out

- A similar upstream report, **llama.cpp#26763**, was closed as *"not a bug"*. The distinction here is that the parser is selected by matching the **source template string**, not the **rendered output**, so a model whose template contains the trigger substrings but renders the delimiters differently is silently mis-routed.

# `ledger_extract.py` records compound-command output as an error, producing a false dev-diary entry

## Summary

`tools/ledger_extract.py` records every `tool_result` with `is_error=true` as `"ERR <first 120 chars>"` without including the command that produced it. Because the exit status of a compound shell command is that of its **last** command, a `grep` that found no match inside a compound command can cause the *search output* (not an error message) to be logged as an error. That truncated, context-free "error" is then fed to `tools/ledger_build.py`, which asks a local model to write a dev-diary entry, resulting in a diary that states things that are not true.

## Reproduction steps

1. Run a compound shell command of the form:
   ```
   grep ... argus/driver.py ...; which faketime
   ```
   where the `grep` portion matches nothing (exit 1) and the `which faketime` portion also exits non-zero, so the compound command's overall exit status is 1.
2. Observe that `ledger_extract.py` records the `tool_result` (the `grep` output — in this case an old docstring on `argus/driver.py` line 9) with `is_error=true`.
3. The entry is stored as `"ERR <first 120 chars>"` of that output, with no record of the originating command.
4. `ledger_build.py` consumes the ledger and asks the local model to write a dev-diary entry.
5. The resulting 2026-09-23 diary states:
   > "argus/driver.py:9 hit a route that exists in no Hermes codebase … Worked around by setting both TZ and HERMES_TIMEZONE"

## Observed behaviour

- The diary entry above was produced, asserting (a) that `argus/driver.py:9` hit a route that exists in no Hermes codebase, and (b) that the issue was worked around by setting both `TZ` and `HERMES_TIMEZONE`.
- Neither claim is true. The "error" was merely the `grep` output (an old docstring), and the `TZ` change was unrelated and was later found to be a bug in its own right.

## Expected behaviour

- `ledger_extract.py` should not record the output of a successful (or merely unmatched) `grep` as an error simply because the *compound* command's exit status is non-zero (the exit status belongs to the last command in the chain).
- The recorded entry should include the command that produced the output so that `ledger_build.py` / the local model has sufficient context to write an accurate diary entry.
- The dev-diary should not contain fabricated root-cause statements or "workarounds" that did not occur.

## Ruled out

- The claim that `argus/driver.py:9` "hit a route that exists in no Hermes codebase" is false; no such route was encountered.
- The `TZ` / `HERMES_TIMEZONE` change is not a valid workaround for the reported issue; it was unrelated and has since been identified as a bug.
- The non-zero exit status is correctly explained by shell semantics: in a compound `cmd1; cmd2` chain, the exit status is that of `cmd2` (`which faketime`), not of the `grep`. The `grep` output itself is not an error condition.

## Error Classification Module

Utilities for triaging shell-command output: deciding whether a non-zero exit code represents a genuine failure, an expected "no match" result, or a benign non-zero exit.

---

### Constants

| Name | Type | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `ERROR_SIG` | `re.Pattern` (case-insensitive) | Matches common error vocabulary in command output (`traceback`, `error`, `exception`, `segfault`, `out of memory`, `timed out`, `refused`, `invalid`, …). |
| `SEARCHY` | `re.Pattern` | Matches commands whose non-zero exit code conventionally means *"nothing matched / files differ / item absent"* rather than *"the command broke"* (`grep`, `rg`, `find`, `test`, `[`, `diff`, `cmp`, `pgrep`, `which`, `command -v`, `git diff`, `git grep`, `git check-ignore`, `git ls-files`, …). An optional absolute or relative path prefix (e.g. `/usr/bin/grep`) is tolerated. |

---

### Functions

#### `last_command(cmd: str | None) -> str`

Extracts the **final segment** of a compound shell command, because in POSIX shells the exit status of a compound command is that of its last command.

**Processing steps (in order):**

1. Split on any of `&&`, `||`, `;`, newline, or `|`; discard empty segments.
2. Take the last segment.
3. Strip well-known leading wrappers:
   - `timeout <duration> `
   - `sudo `
   - `env VAR=VAL … ` (one or more assignments)
   - `! ` (negation)
4. Strip an `ssh [options] user@host '` prefix so the *remote* command is what gets inspected.

**Returns:** the cleaned last-segment string, or `""` if `cmd` is `None`, empty, or contains no recognisable segments.

> **Edge case:** The split is purely textual; it does not understand quotes. A `|` inside single/double quotes will still be treated as a separator.

---

#### `classify_err(text: str, cmd: str | None) -> str`

Classifies a captured command result into one of three labels.

**Decision order (first match wins):**

| # | Condition | Returns | Rationale |
|---|-----------|---------|-----------|
| 1 | `SEARCHY` matches `last_command(cmd)` | `"NONZERO"` | Non-zero is the normal "no match / differs" signal for search & diff tools. |
| 2 | `text` starts with `Exit code 124` **or** contains the literal `<tool_use_error>` | `"FAIL"` | 124 = `timeout` killed the process; `<tool_use_error>` = the harness itself refused the call. |
| 3 | First 400 chars of the body (after stripping a leading `Exit code N` line) match `ERROR_SIG` | `"FAIL"` | The output contains explicit error language. |
| 4 | *(fall-through)* | `"EXIT"` | Non-zero exit with no recognisable error keywords. |

**Parameters**

- `text` – the raw captured output, typically prefixed with `Exit code <n>`.
- `cmd` – the shell command string that produced `text` (or `None`).

**Returns** – one of the strings `"NONZERO"`, `"FAIL"`, `"EXIT"`.

> **Edge case:** Because rule 1 is checked *before* the output is inspected, a `grep` that prints a line containing the word "error" in its own output is still classified `"NONZERO"`.

> **Edge case:** Only the first **400 characters** of the body are searched for `ERROR_SIG`. An error keyword appearing later in a very long output will not trigger `"FAIL"`.

---

#### `content_text(c: str | list | Any) -> str`

Normalises a content payload into a single plain string.

## `signflip_p`

### Purpose

Computes a **sign-flip (permutation) p-value** for the null hypothesis that a dataset is symmetric about zero. The test statistic is the absolute sample mean. The p-value is the proportion of random sign assignments to the (non-zero) observations that yield a statistic at least as extreme as the one observed.

### Parameters

| Name | Type | Description |
|------|------|-------------|
| `ds` | `Sequence[float]` (non-empty) | The observed data. Must support `len()` and iteration. |

### Returns

`tuple[float, str]`

* **p-value** – a float in `[1/(n+1), 1.0]` (Monte Carlo) or `[0, 1.0]` (exact), where *n* = 1 000 000.
* **method label** – `"exact"` or `"monte-carlo 1e6"`, indicating which procedure was used.

### How it works

1. **Observed statistic:** `obs = abs(mean(ds))`.
2. **Non-zero subset:** Values with `|x| ≤ 1e-12` are excluded from sign-flipping (`nz`). They contribute to the denominator (`len(ds)`) but are never re-signed.
3. **Exact enumeration** (when `len(nz) ≤ 22`): All 2^len(nz) sign vectors are enumerated via `itertools.product`. The p-value is the exact fraction of sign vectors whose `|signed mean| ≥ obs − 1e-12`.
4. **Monte Carlo** (when `len(nz) > 22`): 1 000 000 sign vectors are drawn with a **fixed-seed** RNG (`random.Random(0)`, so results are reproducible). The reported p-value is the smoothed estimate `(cnt + 1) / (n + 1)`, which guarantees a lower bound of ≈ 10⁻⁶ and avoids reporting exactly 0.

### Edge cases & notes

* **Empty `ds`** – raises `ZeroDivisionError` (`len(ds) == 0`). The caller must guarantee at least one element.
* **All values near-zero** (`|x| ≤ 1e-12` for every element) – `nz` is empty, the exact branch is taken, the single (empty) sign assignment is counted, and the function returns `(1.0, "exact")`.
* **Floating-point tolerance** – The comparison uses `≥ obs − 1e-12` rather than a strict `≥ obs` to absorb rounding error in the summation.
* **Reproducibility** – The Monte Carlo path is deterministic because the RNG is seeded with `0`. Changing the seed is not exposed as a parameter.
* **Dependencies** – The function assumes `itertools` and `random` are already imported in the calling scope.
* **Scale of the exact branch** – At the upper limit (`len(nz) == 22`) the enumeration visits 2²² ≈ 4.2 million sign vectors. Performance degrades linearly with this count; the Monte Carlo path is used beyond this threshold to keep runtime bounded.
* **Denominator** – The mean is always divided by `len(ds)` (the full sample size), *not* `len(nz)`. Near-zero entries therefore dilute the statistic but do not affect which sign vectors are enumerated.

### Purpose

**KV-cache quantization** shrinks the memory footprint of the key/value tensors the model caches during autoregressive decoding. In FP16, that cache grows linearly with context length and quickly dominates VRAM on a local GPU. Quantizing it to 8-bit or 4-bit (per-channel or per-token scaling factors) cuts that footprint proportionally. The trade-off is a small accuracy loss from the lossy storage; 8-bit is nearly invisible, 4-bit starts to degrade long-context quality noticeably. **Fixed vs. variable bit-rate:** A fixed-rate cache stores every K/V entry at the same precision—say, uniformly 4 bits. Theoretically, speculative decoding is a rejection-sampling identity. The draft (e.g. an MTP head) proposes tokens; the target model scores them. Each proposal is accepted with probability min(1, p_t/p_d), and on rejection you resample from the normalized residual (p_t − p_d)⁺/Z. A standard change-of-measure argument shows the marginal distribution of every emitted token is exactly p_t, so the output *distribution* is provably identical to running the target model alone. No approximation is introduced.

In practice, two things break bit-level equality:

1. **Stochastic sampling consumes the RNG differently.** One draft-verify round draws a different number of random values than the equivalent count of single-step decodes. The per-token marginal is still correct, but the realized sequence will almost certainly differ from a separate baseline run. This is expected, not a bug.

2. **Floating-point non-determinism.** The verification pass is a multi-token forward pass—different batch shape, attention-masking pattern, KV-cache layout, and kernel selection—compared to sequential single-token steps. In FP16/BF16 those reorderings shift the last few ULPs of logits. Near argmax ties or top-k/top-p boundaries that's enough to flip a token. Greedy decoding, which should be deterministic, is the most visibly affected.

The scheme is distributionally exact but not bit-identical.

A MoE layer replaces the FFN with many small FFN "experts" and a lightweight router that, per token, picks the top-*k* experts (e.g., 2 of 32). Only the selected experts' weights are ever used for a given token.

In a RAM-offloaded deployment you keep a subset of experts resident in GPU VRAM (the "hot" set) and park the rest in system DRAM. At inference time the router's decision is trivially fast (a small matmul + softmax). The problem is what follows: if a token is routed to a cold expert, you must DMA that expert's weight tensor (~tens of MB for a 7B-class expert) from DRAM to VRAM over PCIe before the FFN multiply-add can execute. That transfer is the critical-path stall.

Speed is therefore bounded by:

- **PCIe/CXL bandwidth** (≈32 GB/s Gen4, ≈64 GB/s Gen5 x16). A 40 MB expert takes ~0.6–1.2 ms just to land in VRAM.
- **Transfer-to-compute ratio.** With a small batch, you move the full weight matrix to multiply a handful of hidden-state vectors, so you're bandwidth-bound, not FLOP-bound. Larger batches amortize the transfer across more tokens and shift the bottleneck back toward compute.
- **Expert locality / hit rate.** If routing is skewed, a small hot set covers most tokens and cold misses are rare. Uniform routing maximizes misses.
- **Prefetch accuracy.** You can speculatively stream likely experts based on the router's soft probabilities, but a wrong guess wastes bandwidth and adds latency.

In practice the GPU sits idle during each cold-expert fetch, so wall-clock throughput degrades roughly in proportion to the fraction of tokens that hit offloaded experts, scaled by the PCIe transfer time.

**What the label encodes:**

The prefix identifies the quantization *family*. `Q*_K_*` are "K-quants": a two-level hierarchy of 256-element super-blocks containing 32-element sub-blocks, each with its own scale/clip. `IQ*` (or `Q*_0`/`Q*_1` in older naming) are "i-quants" built on E8 lattice quantization with different super-block structures. The digit is a *nominal* bits-per-weight target. The suffix (`M`, `S`, `XXS`, etc.) selects a specific **mixed-precision recipe**: which layers (typically attention projections vs. FFN, or embedding vs. output) get a higher-precision sub-quant (e.g., Q4_K_M pairs Q4_K with Q6_K on select tensors), and what the sub-block grouping is.

**What it does *not* tell you:**

- **Exact bpw.** Q4_K_M is ≈ 4.83 bpw, not 4. You must check the header or compute `filesize / n_params`.
- **Per-layer allocation.** "M" is a convention, not a spec; the exact tensor-to-quant mapping lives in the GGUF metadata and the `llama-quantize` source.
- **Architecture or parameter count.** The label is orthogonal to whether the file is Llama-3-8B or Mistral-7B.
- **Whether embeddings/output are f16.** Some builds keep those unquantized; the label doesn't flag it.
- **Quality.** Two Q4_K_M files of the same base model can differ if built with different `--imatrix` settings or from slightly different checkpoints.

Treat the label as a *family + recipe index*, then read the GGUF tensor metadata for ground truth.

## The actual difficulty: VBR's error is path-dependent

A static codec's error is a function of its **configuration**. VBR's error is a function of its **history**: which layers were shed, at what point in the sequence, and how many times existing tokens were re-encoded along the way.

**Two runs that finish at identical bits/value can have different fidelity**, depending on when the pressure arrived. No single-shot benchmark can distinguish them, because what is being measured is a trajectory, not a state.

This also hurts reproducibility. The budget is derived from **live per-device free memory** (`:1497-1519`). `VBR_BUDGET_MIB` overrides it and is documented as *"forced-budget instrumentation must never grow."* Without that override, **VBR's behaviour depends on what else is resident on the GPU.** Co-tenancy is a first-class concept in this code.

### Our instrument is structurally blind to all of it

`frontier-hazard` builds one context, prefills once, scores, and exits. There is no progressive pressure and no re-encode event, so **the entire mechanism VBR exists for never occurs.** On top of that, at `--n-prefix 128` the cache is 1–4 MiB against a budget in GiB, so the trigger cannot arm even with the env set. Combined with `SCOPE_CORRECTION_136_TOKENS.md`: **VBR is not under-measured by our panels; it is unmeasurable by them.**
